H1.text: Ask three friends to list the good students in your class. You will get three different lists.

H2.text: Now ask them to list the students who ride a bicycle to college. All three lists match, exactly.

H3.text: Aarav noticed this in the college corridor today.

H4.text: Same class, same friends. Why does one list work, and the other one fail?

H5.text: The answer is the very first idea of Class 11 maths. It is called a set.

P2.text: A set is a well defined collection of objects.

P3.text: Well defined means it passes one simple test. For any object, everyone can say clearly: is it in, or is it out?

P4.text: Watch the test run. Our rule is: even numbers less than ten.

P5.text: One? It is odd, so it is out. Two? Even, and less than ten. It is in.

P6.text: Every number gets a clear answer. So the collection is two, four, six and eight. That is a set.

K1.text: Side by side. Students who ride a bicycle. Kiran rides one, so she is in. Joel walks, so he is out. Everyone agrees.

K2.text: Good students. Is Meera good? One friend says yes, another says no. There is no clear answer, so it is not a set.

K3.text: Now you try. Is the collection of months that begin with the letter J a set? Pause and decide.

K4.text: Yes! January, June and July. Anyone who checks a calendar gets the same three months.

E1.text: The objects inside a set are called its elements, or members.

E2.text: We name a set with a capital letter, like A. Its elements are small letters or numbers.

E3.text: If two is in A, we write two, then this curly symbol, then A. It reads: two belongs to A.

E4.text: If three is not in A, we strike the symbol through. Three does not belong to A.

T1.text: Remember this. A set is a collection with a clear in or out answer for every object.

Z1.text: Some sets are used so often that they get their own letters.

Z2.text: N is the natural numbers. One, two, three, and on forever.

Z3.text: Z is the integers. It adds zero and the negative numbers.

Z4.text: Q is the rational numbers. Every number p over q, where p and q are integers and q is not zero.

Z5.text: R is the real numbers. Every single point on the number line.

Z6.text: Quick one. Is zero a natural number? Pause and think.

Z7.text: No! Natural numbers start at one. Zero first appears in Z, the integers.

R1.text: Now, how do we write a set down? There are two ways.

R2.text: The first is roster form. List every element inside curly brackets, with commas between them.

R3.text: Our set becomes two, four, six, eight, inside curly brackets.

R4.text: The second is set builder form. Instead of listing the elements, we write the rule they all follow.

R5.text: Read it like this. The set of all x, such that x is an even natural number, and x is less than ten.

R6.text: The curly bracket means the set of. x stands for any element. The colon means such that. After the colon comes the rule.

R7.text: Now watch the rule do the work. Change the limit from ten to twenty.

R8.text: The rule stays short, but the list keeps growing. That is why set builder form wins for big sets.

S1.text: Side by side. Roster form shows you every element. It is best for small sets.

S2.text: Set builder form shows you the rule. It is best for large or endless sets, like all the real numbers between zero and one.

W2.text: A is the set of all x, such that x is a prime number less than twenty. Write A in roster form. Is nine in A?

W3.text: Step one. A prime number has exactly two factors, one and itself.

W4.text: Step two. Test every number from two to nineteen.

W5.text: Step three. The primes are two, three, five, seven, eleven, thirteen, seventeen and nineteen.

W6.text: Step four. Nine is three times three. It has three factors, so nine does not belong to A.

W7.text: So A has eight elements, and two is the only even one.

X2.text: Write the set of integers x such that x squared is less than ten. Many students write one, two, three.

X3.text: But integers include zero and the negatives. Minus three squared is nine, which is also less than ten. The full set has seven elements, from minus three to three.

J1.text: Where is this asked? In JEE Main, as questions that give a set in set builder form and ask how many elements it has.

Q1.text: Exam level now. How many elements are in this set? Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is C. Twenty five.

A2.text: If n is even, n squared minus one is odd. An odd number is never divisible by eight.

A3.text: If n is odd, n minus one and n plus one are two even numbers in a row. One of them is a multiple of four.

A4.text: So their product is a multiple of two times four, which is eight. Every odd n from one to forty nine works, even one, because zero is divisible by eight. That is twenty five numbers.

F1.text: Here is your recap. Screenshot this card.

Y1.text: Can you answer these three questions without help?

Y2.text: One. Why is good students not a set?

Y3.text: Two. Write the vowels of English in roster form.

Y4.text: Three. What does the colon mean in set builder form?

N1.text: Next time: the word SCHOOL has two O's. So why does its set have only one? We find out in roster and set builder forms.
